# Notes on extension package registration and placement

## Specifying the extension package

All IM-LogicDesigner extension features (flow elements, mapping functions, EL functions, flow triggers) are automatically loaded by the platform, which scans the classpath at startup. The package to scan must be specified explicitly, by implementing a class that provides the specification.

The specified package is searched including its subpackages. **If the scanned range is too broad, startup analysis can take longer**, so keep the specified package as narrow as possible.

The class that specifies the package implements the `jp.co.intra_mart.system.logic.factory.ElementScanPackageFactory` interface.

```java
package org.example.logicdesigner;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Collection;

import jp.co.intra_mart.system.logic.factory.ElementScanPackageFactory;

public class MyPackageFactory implements ElementScanPackageFactory {

    @Override
    public Collection<String> getTargetPackages() {
        return Arrays.asList("org.example.logicdesigner");
    }
}
```

- Enumerate the package names to scan as strings in the return value of `getTargetPackages()`
- Place the category, flow element, and metadata classes you create afterward under the package specified here (including subpackages)

## Placing the ServiceLoader provider configuration file

The package factory class you create is treated as a service provider loaded via `java.util.ServiceLoader`. You therefore need to place the following provider configuration file on the classpath.

```
src/main/resources/META-INF/services/jp.co.intra_mart.system.logic.factory.ElementScanPackageFactory
```

The file's content is a single line containing the fully qualified class name (FQCN) of the package factory class you created.

```
org.example.logicdesigner.MyPackageFactory
```

**One such file is enough per project.** When adding multiple flow elements/tasks under the same package, you do not need to create the `ElementScanPackageFactory` implementation and this provider configuration file again — just add classes under the existing scanned package if the project already has one.

## Placement on the runtime classpath

The Java classes you create (category, flow element, metadata, and package factory classes) must have their compiled `.class` files (or a JAR containing them) **present on the application server's runtime classpath**. Placing only source files does not make them work.

The specific placement method (placing a JAR under WEB-INF/lib, deploying as an OSGi bundle module, etc.) depends on the project's build configuration and is out of scope for this skill. Follow the project's existing Java module build/deploy procedure. If no existing Java module exists, confirm the following with the user.

1. Which Maven module (or new module) to add the Java source to
2. How to reflect the build artifact (JAR) into the deployment environment

## Difference from IM-Workflow's Java integration

The Java classes generated by `java-im-workflow-usage` are only invoked once the implementation class's FQCN is registered as a string in `plugins[].parameter` of the workflow definition (import XML).

By contrast, the flow elements targeted by this skill are loaded via **automatic scanning driven by the `@LogicFlowElement` annotation and `ElementScanPackageFactory`**. There is no step to individually register an FQCN in an XML file or elsewhere. Placing a class annotated with `@LogicFlowElement` under the scanned package is enough for it to automatically appear on the palette at startup.

## Instantiation conditions for the class

A flow element class instance is created for every logic flow execution (though the instance is reused when the same flow element is invoked repeatedly, e.g. inside a loop). Since `Task`'s constructor takes an `ElementContext` argument, unlike IM-Workflow's Java integration (which requires a no-argument constructor), **you do not need to provide a no-argument constructor**.
